function_statements.text: Bifunctional enzyme with both catalase and broad-spectrum peroxidase activity, oxidizing various electron donors including NADP(H) (PubMed:18178143, PubMed:9006925). Protects M.tuberculosis against toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS) including hydrogen peroxide as well as organic peroxides and thus contributes to its survival within host macrophages by countering the phagocyte oxidative burst (PubMed:15165233, PubMed:8658136). Also displays efficient peroxynitritase activity, which may help the bacterium to persist in macrophages (PubMed:10080924)

Might be involved in DNA repair. Partly complements recA-deficient E.coli cells exposed to UV radiation, mitomycin C or hydrogen peroxide. Increases resistance to mitomycin C in E.coli cells deficient for either uvrA, uvrB or uvrC

Catalyzes the oxidative activation of the antitubercular pro-drug isoniazid (INH) to generate an isonicotinoyl radical that then reacts nonenzymatically with NAD to form an isonicotinoyl-NAD adduct which inhibits InhA

detail.matched_passage:
AhpC, oxidative stress and drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

The Mycobacterium tuberculosis AhpC is similar to a family of bacterial and eukaryotic antioxidant proteins with alkylhydroperoxidase (Ahp) and thioredoxin-dependent peroxidase (TPx) activities. AhpC expression is associated with resistance to the front-line antitubercular drug isoniazid in the naturally resistant organisms E. coli and M. smegmatis. We identified several isoniazid-resistant M. tuberculosis isolates with ahpC promoter mutations resulting in AhpC overexpression. These strains were more resistant to cumene hydroperoxide than were wild-type strains. However, these strains were unchanged in their sensitivity to isoniazid, refuting a role for AhpC in detoxification of this drug. All the isoniazid-resistant, AhpC-overexpressing strains were also deficient in activity of the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase KatG. KatG, the only known catalase in M. tuberculosis, is required for activation of isoniazid. We propose that compensatory ahpC promoter mutations are selected from KatG-deficient, isoniazid-resistant M. tuberculosis during infections, to mitigate the added burden imposed by organic peroxides on these strains.

detail.matched_passage: Genetic mutations underlying isoniazid-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. Tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is a major public health issue in Pakistan. Isoniazid is a first-line pro-drug that requires activation through an enzyme called catalase peroxidase, but is subject to widespread resistance, driven by mutations in katG and inhA genes and other loci with compensatory effects (e.g., ahpC). Here, we used whole genome sequencing data from 51 M. tuberculosis isolates collected from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province (years 2016-2019; all isoniazid phenotypically resistant) to investigate the genetic diversity of mutations in isoniazid candidate genes. The most common mutations underlying resistance were katG S315T (37/51), fabG1 -15C>T (13/51; inhA promoter), and inhA -154G>A (7/51). Other less common mutations (n < 5) were also identified in katG (R128Q, V1A, W505*, A109T, D311G) and candidate compensatory genes ahpC (-54C>T, -51G>A) and oxyS (M249T). Using DynaMut2 software, the mutants exhibited various degrees of stability and flexibility on protein structures, with some katG mutations leading to a decrease in KatG protein flexibility. Overall, the characterisation of circulating isoniazid resistant-linked mutations will assist in drug resistant TB

detail.matched_passage: An upstream truncation of the furA-katG operon confers high-level isoniazid resistance in a Mycobacterium tuberculosis clinical isolate with no known resistance-associated mutations. Although the major causes of isoniazid (INH) resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis are confined to structural mutations in katG and promoter mutations in the mabA-inhA operon, a significant proportion of INH-resistant strains have unknown resistance mechanisms. Recently, we identified a high-level INH-resistant M. tuberculosis clinical isolate, GB005, with no known resistance-associated mutations. A comprehensive study was performed to investigate the molecular basis of drug resistance in this strain. Although no mutations were found throughout the katG and furA-katG intergenic region, the katG expression and the catalase activity were greatly diminished compared to those in H37Rv (P < 0.01). Northern blotting revealed that the katG transcript from the isolate was smaller than that of H37Rv. Sequencing analysis of furA and upstream genes discovered a 7.2-kb truncation extended from the 96th base preceding the initiation codon of katG. Complementation of the M. tuberculosis Δ(furA-katG) strain with katG and different portions of the truncated region identified a 134-bp upstream fragment of furA
detail.quotable_text: An upstream truncation of the furA-katG operon confers high-level isoniazid resistance in a Mycobacterium tuberculosis clinical isolate with no known resistance-associated mutations. Although the major causes of isoniazid (INH) resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis are confined to structural mutations in katG and promoter mutations in the mabA-inhA operon, a significant proportion of INH-resistant strains have unknown resistance mechanisms. Recently, we identified a high-level INH-resistant M. tuberculosis clinical isolate, GB005, with no known resistance-associated mutations. A comprehensive study was performed to investigate the molecular basis of drug resistance in this strain. Although no mutations were found throughout the katG and furA-katG intergenic region, the katG expression and the catalase activity were greatly diminished compared to those in H37Rv (P < 0.01). Northern blotting revealed that the katG transcript from the isolate was smaller than that of H37Rv. Sequencing analysis of furA and upstream genes discovered a 7.2-kb truncation extended from the 96th base preceding the initiation codon of katG. Complementation of the M. tuberculosis Δ(furA-katG) strain with katG and different portions of the truncated region identified a 134-bp upstream fragment of furA upstream genes discovered a 7.2-kb truncation extended from the 96th base preceding the initiation codon of katG. Complementation of the M. tuberculosis Δ(furA-katG) strain with katG and different portions of the truncated region identified a 134-bp upstream fragment of furA that was essential for full catalase activity and INH susceptibility in M. tuberculosis. The promoter activity of this fragment was also shown to be stronger than that of the furA-katG intergenic region (P < 0.01). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that deletion of the 134-bp furA upstream fragment is responsible for the reduction in katG expression, resulting in INH resistance in GB005. To our knowledge, this is the first report showing that deletion of the upstream region preceding the furA-katG operon causes high-level INH resistance in a clinical isolate of M. tuberculosis.

METHODS: A total of 101 isoniazid-resistant and 43 susceptible strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis were analyzed by PCR and sequence analysis of their katG, inhA, ahpC, kasA, and oxyR genes. RESULTS: (1) Sequencing of katG from 101 INH-resistant strains showed point mutations, small deletions or insertions in 81 isolates (80.2%), but no complete deletions were identified. Low level isoniazid resistant strains (1 microg/ml) had higher mutation frequency at 315-Ser than high level isoniazid resistant strains (10 microg/ml; chi(2) = 9.31, P < 0.05). detail.quotable_text: Genetic Characterization Conferred Co-Resistance to Isoniazid and Ethionamide in Mycobacterium tuberculosis Isolates from Southern Xinjiang, China. BACKGROUND: Ethionamide (ETH), a structural analogue of isoniazid (INH), is used for treating multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Due to the common target InhA, INH and ETH showed cross-resistance in M. tuberculosis. This study aimed to explore the INH and ETH resistant profiles and genetic mutations conferring independent INH- or ETH-resistance and INH-ETH cross-resistance in M. tuberculosis circulating in south of Xinjiang, China. METHODS: From Sep 2017 to Dec 2018, 312 isolates were included using drug susceptibility testing (DST), spoligotyping, and whole genome sequencing (WGS) to analyze the resistance characteristics for INH and/or ETH. RESULTS: Among the 312 isolates, 185 (58.3%) and 127 (40.7%) belonged to the Beijing family and non-Beijing family, respectively; 90 (28.9%) were INH-resistant (INHR) with mutation rates of 74.4% in katG, 13.3% in inhA and its promoter, 11.1% in ahpC and its upstream region, 2.2% in ndh, 0.0% in mshA, whilst 34 (10.9%) were ETH-resistant (ETHR) with mutation rates of 38.2% in ethA, 26.2% in inhA and its promoter, and 5.9% in in inhA and its promoter, 11.1% in ahpC and its upstream region, 2.2% in ndh, 0.0% in mshA, whilst 34 (10.9%) were ETH-resistant (ETHR) with mutation rates of 38.2% in ethA, 26.2% in inhA and its promoter, and 5.9% in ndh, 0.0% in ethR or mshA; and 25 (8.0%) were INH-ETH co-resistant (INHRETHR) with mutation rates of 40.0% in inhA and its promoter, and 8% in ndh. katG mutants tended to display high-level resistant to INH; and more inhA and its promoter mutants showed low-level of INH and ETH resistance. summary:
## Genes

**katG (Rv1908c)** — catalase-peroxidase. UniProt P9WIE5, experimental tier: *"Bifunctional enzyme with both catalase and broad-spectrum peroxidase activity"* and *"Protects M.tuberculosis against toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS) including hydrogen peroxide as well as organic peroxides"*; also *"Catalyzes the oxidative activation of the antitubercular pro-drug isoniazid (INH)"*. Homodimer.

**ahpC (Rv2428)** — alkyl hydroperoxide reductase C. UniProt P9WQB7, experimental tier: *"Thiol-specific peroxidase that catalyzes the reduction of hydrogen peroxide and organic hydroperoxides to water and alcohols"*, and notably *"Does not however seem to play a role in detoxification of isoniazid"*. Dodecamer; complexes with AhpD, DlaT, Lpd.

## Confounding check (lineage markers) — run for both, as required

- **katG**: no lineage-defining position falls within the gene in the tbdb barcode (informative negative; 855/4,008 genes carry one).
- **ahpC**: same — negative.

Neither gene carries a barcode position, so the single most common confound in a clinical-isolate epistasis scan — two lineage markers co-segregating with population structure — is **not** supported here. That does not fully exonerate the association: katG and ahpC variants both cluster in INH-resistant, often clonally expanded MDR backgrounds, so residual relatedness/treatment-history confounding remains a live alternative and should be tested by conditioning on genome-wide relatedness and on INH phenotype, not on lineage calls alone.

## Resistance catalogue (run for both)

- **katG**: **resistance-associated**, drug **isoniazid**. 1,771 catalogued variants; 139 graded associated (10 "Assoc w R", 129 "Assoc w R - Interim"), against 7 "Not assoc w R", 236 "Not assoc w R - Interim", 1,254 "Uncertain significance", 135 ungraded. Associated entries include whole-gene loss-of-function classes (`tbdb:katG:transcript_ablation`, `tbdb:katG:frameshift_variant`, `tbdb:katG:stop_gained`, `tbdb:katG:start_lost`) and `tbdb:katG:p.Ser315Thr`. This is a statement about the gene; it does not grade any particular variant you may have flagged.
- **ahpC**: **present in the catalogue and assessed, but negative** — 250 variants, none graded associated (2 "Not assoc w R", 56 "Not assoc w R - Interim", 181 "Uncertain significance", 11 ungraded). This is the "assessed and came back negative" case, not "never assessed".

That asymmetry is itself the most informative structured result: one partner is a graded resistance determinant, the other is explicitly not.

## Interpreting the pair

The deterministic verdict is a **direct STRING edge, combined 0.968, with `evidence_beyond_textmining: false`** (textmining 0.965, best non-textmining channel 0.096) and **no shared pathway**. I will not upgrade that. STRING here is recording that katG and ahpC are named together in enormous numbers of papers, not that any experimental or curated-database channel links the proteins. The papers I retrieved are very likely the *source* of that textmining score, so they and the STRING edge are **one line of evidence — literature — not two**.

What that literature says about the relationship is nonetheless specific and mechanistically coherent, and it is an *epistatic* relationship rather than a physical one:

- PMID:10609885 "We identified several isoniazid-resistant M. tuberculosis isolates with ahpC promoter mutations resulting in AhpC overexpression" and "All the isoniazid-resistant, AhpC-overexpressing strains were also deficient in activity of the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase KatG", concluding "We propose that compensatory ahpC promoter mutations are selected from KatG-deficient, isoniazid-resistant M. tuberculosis during infections, to mitigate the added burden imposed by organic peroxides on these strains."
- The same paper is explicit that this is not drug detoxification: "these strains were unchanged in their sensitivity to isoniazid, refuting a role for AhpC in detoxification of this drug."
- PMID:36463715 frames ahpC the same way in modern WGS surveys: resistance is "driven by mutations in katG and inhA genes and other loci with compensatory effects (e.g., ahpC)", with "candidate compensatory genes ahpC (-54C>T, -51G>A)".

**Kind of link.** Not a direct physical interaction — nothing in the retrieved evidence supports contact between the two proteins, and their known quaternary structures are separate (KatG homodimer; AhpC dodecamer in a complex with AhpD/DlaT/Lpd). Not a shared annotated pathway — the table says shared pathways: none, and I found no basis to claim otherwise. The defensible reading is **shared biochemical function with a compensatory, epistatic genetic relationship**: both enzymes detoxify hydrogen and organic peroxides (per the two UniProt experimental statements above), so loss of KatG leaves a peroxide-detoxification deficit that upregulated AhpC can offset. An upstream epistasis scan over clinical isolates is exactly the design that would surface this, because the two loci' genotypes are non-independent through selection, not through a protein complex.

**A caution on the shared neighbourhood.** The ten shared partners returned — 83332.Rv0432 (sodC), 83332.Rv0667 (rpoB), 83332.Rv1483 (fabG1), 83332.Rv1484 (inhA), 83332.Rv1854c (ndh), 83332.Rv1909c (furA), 83332.Rv2043c (pncA), 83332.Rv2245 (kasA), 83332.Rv3795 (embB), 83332.Rv3846 (sodA) — are dominated by first- and second-line drug-resistance genes across unrelated drugs (rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol). That pattern is what you expect from a neighbourhood assembled largely by co-mention in drug-resistance papers, and both partner lists hit the retrieval limit of 20, so true degree is unknown and the overlap fraction cannot be interpreted. I would not read this overlap as a functional module. The two exceptions worth noting on prior functional grounds are furA (the gene immediately upstream of katG; PMID:25092698 studies "the furA-katG operon" and shows a "134-bp upstream fragment of furA that was essential for full catalase activity and INH susceptibility") and the superoxide dismutases, which sit in the same oxidative-stress problem space — but I retrieved no channel-level evidence for those specific edges here.

## What would test the link

Genotype-level: check whether ahpC promoter variants in your isolates occur preferentially on katG loss-of-function backgrounds and are near-absent on katG-wild-type backgrounds, and whether the interaction survives conditioning on genome-wide relatedness and on INH phenotype. Phenotype-level: the prediction from PMID:10609885 is specific and falsifiable — ahpC-overexpressing strains should gain organic-peroxide resistance ("These strains were more resistant to cumene hydroperoxide than were wild-type strains") without any change in INH MIC.
